extracted.intended_audience: high-school and early undergraduate students, math-contest participants and coaches (AIME/AMC/ARML level)
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpt from a trigonometry/problem-solving textbook presenting definitions, identities, geometric constructions, vector and complex-number techniques, and worked contest-style examples for solving trig and analytic geometry problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brocard point definition and uniqueness
rubrics_metrics.description: Point P inside triangle ABC such that angles PAB, PBC, and PCA are all congruent; the Brocard point is unique and the second Brocard point satisfies similar relations in reverse order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct the Brocard point by constructing the circle through A and tangent to AB at A (from equation ∠PAB = ∠PCA) and the circle through B tangent to AC at C (from ∠PBC = ∠PCA); the Brocard point lies at the unique intersection (other than the tangent point) of these circles. The two Brocard points are isogonal conjugates (reflect AP, BP, CP across the angle bisectors and use Ceva's theorem). Example: AIME 1999 problem computing Brocard angle for sides 13,14,15.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation between Brocard angle and triangle sides (tan/cot identity)
rubrics_metrics.description: An identity relating the Brocard angle α (where ∠PAB = ∠PBC = ∠PCA = α) to side lengths and area: the text states the rearranged relation as 2 tan α = 4[ABC] / (a^2 + b^2 + c^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive via law of cosines on triangles PAB, PBC, PCA, summation, and expression of combined areas: 2(cx + ay + bz) cos α = a^2 + b^2 + c^2 and combined area = (cx+ay+bz) sin α, leading to the displayed relation. Applied numerically in the AIME example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cotangent expansion for Brocard angle
rubrics_metrics.description: cot α = (a^2 + b^2 + c^2) / (4[ABC]) = (sin^2 A + sin^2 B + sin^2 C) / (2 sin A sin B sin C)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use law of sines to express a^2/(2bc sin A) etc., giving the symmetric expansion in terms of side lengths or sines of angles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cosecant-squared Brocard identity
rubrics_metrics.description: csc^2 α = csc^2 A + csc^2 B + csc^2 C (for the Brocard angle α and triangle angles A,B,C).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived by expressing areas of triangles CAP, ABP, BCP as [ABC]·sin^2 α / sin^2 (corresponding angle) and summing to recover identity; equality condition and intermediate steps shown in the worked example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vector definition and notation
rubrics_metrics.description: A vector from point A=(x1,y1) to B=(x2,y2) is written AB→ = [x2 − x1, y2 − y1]; vectors are represented as directed segments with a tail and head.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vectors can be added geometrically (parallelogram rule), and scaling c·[a,b] = [ca,cb]; placing tails at origin gives head coordinates equal to the vector components. Examples with coordinates provided (Figure 1.43, Example 1.14).

rubrics_metrics.name: Vector addition and scalar multiplication (component rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: If u=[a,b] and v=[m,n], then u+v=[a+m,b+n] and c·u=[ca,cb]; collinearity occurs if one vector is a scalar multiple of another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric parallelogram interpretation: OA + OB = OC in parallelogram OAEB. Examples show computing intermediate positions given motion vectors and time fractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vector magnitude and slope; perpendicularity criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: The magnitude |u| of vector u=[a,b] is sqrt(a^2+b^2); the slope is b/a when a≠0. Two vectors u=[a,b] and v=[m,n] are perpendicular iff am + bn = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perpendicularity can be derived from the Pythagorean relation |u|^2 + |v|^2 = |u−v|^2 or via slope product = −1. Examples and geometric illustrations are provided (Figure 1.44).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dot product definition and basic properties
rubrics_metrics.description: For u=[a,b] and v=[m,n], define u·v = am + bn. Properties: (i) v·v = |v|^2 ≥ 0; (ii) u·v = v·u; (iii) u·(v+w)=u·v+u·w; (iv) (c u)·v = c(u·v).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These properties extend straightforwardly to higher dimensions; used repeatedly to relate algebraic computations to geometry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dot product and angle (vector form of law of cosines)
rubrics_metrics.description: If u and v are placed tail-to-tail and form angle θ, then cos θ = (u·v)/(|u||v|), and equivalently |v − u|^2 = |u|^2 + |v|^2 − 2|u||v| cos θ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive by applying the law of cosines to triangle formed by vector heads; this relation is used to compute angles and distances between vectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cauchy–Schwarz inequality (vector/real sequences)
rubrics_metrics.description: (am + bn)^2 ≤ (a^2 + b^2)(m^2 + n^2) (2D case); generalized: (∑ai^2)(∑bi^2) ≥ (∑aibi)^2 for real ai,bi. Equality iff the vectors are proportional (ai/bi constant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via dot-product/angle argument (|cos θ| ≤ 1). Example application given (Example 1.11) with equality condition specified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Radian measure and basic conversions
rubrics_metrics.description: Radian measure: π radians = 180°; arc length for central angle y (radians) on circle of radius R is yR; sector area is (1/2) R^2 y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why radian measure is advantageous for algebraic relations in trigonometry and gives examples of special-angle radian measures to memorize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric inequality sin θ < θ < tan θ for 0<θ<π/2
rubrics_metrics.description: For 0 < θ < π/2, sin θ < θ < tan θ, with geometric proof using unit circle, chords and tangents; consequence: lim_{θ→0} (sin θ)/θ = 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare areas of triangle OAB, sector OAB, and triangle OAD to get the inequality; use squeeze theorem with sec θ → 1 to conclude the limit. Notes that directions (positive/negative) are handled in calculus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing sinusoidal curves via cylinder cut (unrolling argument)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cutting a cylindrical surface at an angle and unrolling the paper produces a sinusoidal curve; for the presented configuration, the unrolled curve is y = 1 + cos x (or y = 2 + cos x if bottom not removed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set coordinates on unrolled paper with arc-length parameter θ mapped to x coordinate; show BD = 1 + cos θ so that D1 = (θ, 1 + cos θ). Example demonstrates symmetry choices and coordinate placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: 3-D rectangular (Cartesian) coordinates and distances
rubrics_metrics.description: Point P=(x,y,z) with distances to coordinate planes/axes given by combinations of coordinates; distance between P1=(x1,y1,z1) and P2=(x2,y2,z2) is sqrt((x1−x2)^2+(y1−y2)^2+(z1−z2)^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by box ABCDEFGH example; shows how to visualize axes in a room and relate coordinates to directed distances from coordinate planes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spherical coordinates and conversion to rectangular
rubrics_metrics.description: Spherical coordinates (r, α, β) with α = longitude, β = latitude: rectangular conversion E=(r cos α cos β, r sin α cos β, r sin β).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply to Earth model (r=3960 miles) and derive coordinates for points given latitude/longitude; explains sign conventions and ranges for latitudes/longitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Great-circle geodesics as shortest surface paths
rubrics_metrics.description: Shortest path between two points on a sphere lies along a great circle (intersection of sphere with a plane through center); as radius→∞ the great circle arc approaches a straight segment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why airline routes often use high-latitude great-circle arcs and suggests drawing great circles through sample points on a globe to visualize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spherical central-angle (dot-product) formula for surface distance
rubrics_metrics.description: For points A=3960(cos α1 cos β1, sin α1 cos β1, sin β1) and B similarly, cos θ = cos α1 cos β1 cos α2 cos β2 + sin α1 cos β1 sin α2 cos β2 + sin β1 sin β2, where θ = ∠AOB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Then surface distance = (θ/360°)·2π·3960. Applied numerically to compute distance between Shanghai and Albany in Example 1.21.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point division along a great-circle arc (interpolation via linear combination)
rubrics_metrics.description: To find point C that divides arc AB with ∠AOC = k∠AOB (k∈[0,1]) represent vector w = OC as w = a u + b v (u=OA, v=OB). Solve linear system cos(kθ)=a + b cos θ and cos((1−k)θ)=a cos θ + b (with |u|=|v|), then compute w = au + bv and convert to spherical coordinates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example computes the 4/5 point (k=4/5) along Shanghai→Albany route, solving for a≈0.376 and b≈1.035 and giving resulting longitude/latitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex-number plane and operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret complex number z=a+bi as point (a,b) in the complex plane; addition corresponds to vector addition; magnitude |z|=sqrt(a^2+b^2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric parallelogram interpretation: OZ1ZZ2 is a parallelogram for z=z1+z2. Examples given with coordinates and diagrams (Figure 1.58).

rubrics_metrics.name: Polar form and De Moivre (r cis θ)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write z = r(cos θ + i sin θ) = r cis θ where r=|z| and θ is the polar angle; De Moivre's formula relates powers/roots via polar representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: −1+√3 i = 2 cis 120°. Properties of adding equal-magnitude complex numbers: sum lies along the bisector and yields half-angle/trigonometric identities such as tan(a/2)=sin a/(1+cos a) and magnitude r' = 2 cos(a/2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem-solving technique: provide two parallel solution approaches (vector and trig)
rubrics_metrics.description: For many problems (examples shown), provide two solutions: one via vector/analytic-geometry methods and another via trigonometric computations, to illustrate multiple approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrating this technique: Example 1.15 (isosceles right triangle locus) and Example 1.16 (mirror slope) present both vector and trigonometric solutions, showing when each method is convenient.
